title: Chapter 147 – A Sister's Path
html:
[Lin Garden – Lin Yue]

On the morning she decides, Yue lies in bed with her eyes closed and listens to the house wake up.

She has done it for fifty-seven years, and she has never once found the end of it. First the rooster, a harsh flat note at the far side of the village, then the answering dogs. The scrape of the bolt on the kitchen door. Her mother's feet on the boards, quick and light, and the dull clink of the kettle on its hook. Somewhere above, a small child coughs and is hushed. Rain ticks on the tiles. A door bangs. The whole Garden fills slowly with its thousand small noises, like a bowl filling with water, and under all of it, deep and steady as a pulse, runs the other sound, the one she was born hearing and has never been able to explain: the long low hum of the seams.

She has always thought of the two as one music. She is about to find out that they are not.

"Mother." It is Zhao, at the door, with the baby on her hip. "You are awake. Grandmother says breakfast."

"I am coming."

"You've been lying there for an hour. I could hear you not-moving." Zhao frowns. "Are you well?"

"Very."

"Because you've the look."

"What look?"

"The one Uncle gets." The young woman shifts Kuang to the other hip. He is a round, grave child of three months, with a fuzz of black hair and his great-uncle's absorbed gaze, and he stares at Yue as he stares at everything, as though trying to work out how it is made. "The one where you've decided to do something silly and you're waiting for someone to stop you."

Yue sits up. She looks at her daughter, at the small solemn face of the grandson, at the pale rain-light coming through the shutter.

"No one is going to stop me," she says. "I think that is rather the point."

* * *

Jian gives her the jar at the end of the month, as he promised, in the Dock.

It is a plain gray ceramic thing, the twin of the one that held the Hollow Gold, no bigger than a rice bowl, with a wax seal and a mark scratched on the lid. A spiral, open at one end, like a snail's shell. She knows the symbol. She has seen it in her sleep.

She stands in front of the cot where her brother has been living for a month, with her hands folded, and says nothing. He sits on the cot with the jar on his knees. He looks tired. The Seed is eating him, slowly, a little each night. His hair is white as paper, and the lines on his face have deepened, and when he looks up at her his eyes are very dark.

"I have to tell you everything I know," he says. "It is not much."

"Tell me."

"There is a note." He tips the lid and takes out a folded strip of paper, brown and soft with age, and holds it out to her. She takes it. The writing is a quick untidy scrawl, the same hand as all the others, and she reads it twice.

For the one who hears. Sorry. It trades what you use for what you were meant to.

She folds it and puts it in her sleeve.

"That is all?"

"That is all. There is what's in the jar." He opens it. Inside, packed in gray salt, lies a small curled thing of pale silver, the length of her thumb. It is shaped like an ear, a delicate, coiled, perfect ear, with the whorls and folds of the real thing, and when she bends over it she can hear, very faintly, a hum, like wind in a keyhole.

"It is a seam," says Jian. "A small one. Alive. I have no idea what it will do to you."

"I'll take it."

"Yue—"

"I know." She smiles. "You are going to say it has a price. Of course it has a price. Everything in this family has a price, and we have all been paying it for years." She touches his white hair, quickly, awkwardly, the way she did when she was thirteen and he came home from the Sect with his face split. "You did not decide this, little brother. I did. I have been listening to that hum for thirty years. I want to know what it is for."

He nods. He does not argue. She loves him for it.

"When?" he says.

"Not yet." She straightens. "There is something I need to do first."

* * *

She goes to Feng that evening, because he is the only other person in the Garden who knows what it is to hear too much.

He is on the porch of the old house, wrapped in two blankets, with his feet on a brazier and his head tilted to the left. He does not turn when she sits down. "I heard," he says. "Jian told Father. Father told Mother. Mother told the cat." A dry laugh. "You've made a good deal of noise for a woman who doesn't like attention."

"It was not my intention."

"It never is." He pours her a cup of tea from the pot at his elbow, and she takes it, and they sit in the dusk for a time without speaking. Rain is coming. She can feel it in the seam of the hill.

"Is it bad?" she says. "What you hear?"

"Which part?"

"All of it."

"Not bad." He considers. "It's like living next to a river. At first you can't think. Then you can't sleep. Then one day, you realize you've stopped noticing, and you can't remember what it was like when the river wasn't there." He turns his face at last. His eyes, in the failing light, are gentle and faintly unfocused. "I don't sleep much. You know that. I don't mind. I lie in the dark and listen to the house, and the fields, and I think, there is so much going on. So much that nobody else can hear. It's a kind of company."

"And if it stopped?"

"Then I'd be lonely." He says it simply. "But it won't. It never does. That's the thing nobody tells you. Once you hear it, you can't stop hearing it. There's no door that goes back."

She looks at the cup in her hands. The steam rises, curls, vanishes.

"I think," she says slowly, "that I would like to be a person who didn't want to go back."

"Then you already are." Feng reaches over, clumsily, and squeezes her hand. His own is thin and dry as paper. "That's the whole trick, little sister. You've been hearing it all your life. You were just never allowed to listen."

* * *

She spends three days saying goodbye to sound.

She does not tell anyone why. She says only that she wants to visit, and the family, who have long ago learned not to press her, let her wander. She goes to the kitchen at dawn and sits at the table with her chin in her hands, and watches her mother cook. Qinghe is at the hob, in her blue smock, humming something tuneless, stirring a pot she cannot taste. She hums constantly. She does not know she does it. It is a small flat cheerful drone, almost a purr, a sound that Yue has heard every morning of her life and never once listened to.

She listens now. She listens to every note.

On the second day she goes to the school, where thirty children sit in rows chanting the Founders' sentence in a ragged chorus, and she stands at the back for an hour with her eyes shut. On the third she sits with her father. Wenyuan is ninety-nine and sleeps a great deal, now, in the chair by the window, wrapped in quilts. When she sits down beside him he wakes, and looks at her, and says, "Well, little bell," and she laughs, helplessly, because he has not called her that since she was seven.

"Father. Say something."

"What shall I say?"

"Anything. Tell me the story of the Stranger. The one in the blue smock."

"You have heard it a hundred times."

"Tell it again."

So he does. It is a very old story, and he tells it in the rusty gentle voice of a man who has told it to three generations of children: the tall stranger who came to the Orchard in a hard winter, with a scar on his palm and spectacles on his nose, who ate three bowls of soup and fell asleep by the fire, and in the morning left a seedling in a pot, and a promise. A long way back, he said. A long way forward. You will not see the end of it. Tend the tree. Her father's voice rises and falls with the words, soft as a worn sleeve, and she sits with her hands in her lap and drinks it in, every breath, every pause, every catch of the old throat.

When he finishes she is crying.

"There now," says Wenyuan. He pats her knee. "It is only an apple."

"I know."

"It is a good apple."

"I know, Father."

"Little bell." His cold hand closes over hers. "Whatever you are about to do, you do it with all our hearts. You always did. I never did understand you, and I never had to. That is the thing about a bell. You do not understand it. You only hear it from a long way off, and you know where home is."

She puts her head down on his knee. She stays there a long time.

* * *

On the evening of the third day, the family gathers in the long hall, and she asks each of them for one sentence.

She does not explain. She only sits at the head of the table, with a lamp in front of her and a bowl of her mother's soup, and says, "Please. Anything you like. Say it to me, one at a time, and say it slowly."

They look at each other. Then Qinghe, who has never in her life needed to be told twice, puts down her spoon and says, in her brisk dry voice, "Eat. It is getting cold."

Yue laughs. She lifts a spoonful of soup. "That one," she says. "That's exactly the one."

Feng, who has been silent, clears his throat. He is seventy-eight, thin as a rail, with a gray-streaked braid and eyes that are always a little unfocused, now, as if looking at something past the room. "I'm proud of you, little sister," he says. It comes out gruff. "I don't think I have ever said it. I should have."

Zhao says, "Mother, you are the best person I know," and Bell, from the far end, blushes scarlet and mumbles that she agrees. The baby gurgles. Lin Kuang's father says, awkwardly, that he is honored to be in the family, and Wenyuan tells him not to be silly. A cousin laughs. Somebody drops a bowl.

And at the foot of the table, a quiet figure in a brown cloak with his white hair tied back, her brother says nothing at all. He only looks at her. After a moment, she understands.

"I know," she says. "You don't have to."

"I wanted to give you a voice to keep. I can't think of a single thing that's good enough."

"Then say my name."

"Yue."

It is the simplest word in the language. He says it very softly, as one sets down a cup, and she shuts her eyes and holds it in her head: the particular weight of it, the little catch before the vowel, the tenderness hiding under the plainness. Yue. She will remember it. She will remember it as long as she remembers anything.

"Thank you," she says. "That's the one."

* * *

She takes the ear into herself on the first night of the dark moon, in the Dock, with the whole family looking on.

It is not like a pill. There is no cocoon, no furnace, no violent tide. Jian says so, several times, as though trying to reassure her, and she nods and does not believe him. She sits on the flat stone before the Gate wall with her legs crossed and her hands in her lap, and her brother sits on the cot behind her with his hand on the Seed, and Pebble, with his cracked back and his small black eyes, perches on her knee.

"I will be with you," says Pebble.

"I know."

"The thing will go down. It is alive, and it will want to settle. Let it."

"I will."

"And Yue." The creature hesitates. "When it is done, there will be a great silence. It will frighten you. It frightened me, when I first woke. Listen through it. There is always a way through."

She nods. She takes the silver ear in her palm and looks at it for a moment: delicate, curled, whispering. She thinks of her mother's humming, her father's story, her brother's voice. She thinks of Kuang, who never in his life said more than he needed to. She puts the ear to her own, the left one, and presses.

It sinks in like a drop of water into sand.

* * *

The first thing that happens is that the sound gets louder.

It swells and swells, until it is impossibly vast: the roar of the cellar seam, the sigh of the roots under the orchard, the voice of the Gate wall, which she has always heard as a murmur and now hears as a hundred voices singing in a hundred different keys. She claps her hands over her ears. She screams. She cannot hear herself do it. All she can hear is the song, endless and enormous and beautiful, and under it, in the heart of it, a single clear rising note that is her own blood.

Listen, says Pebble, from very far away. Through it. Through.

She listens.

It is like walking through a field of tall grass with the wind blowing. She parts the sound with her hands. Layer after layer, voice after voice, the cellar, the roots, the Gate, the Mother Tree, the bell, and behind them, quiet and patient and unending, the great slow chord of the world itself. She has been hearing the edge of it all her life. Now she is standing in the middle.

And the other sounds, the ordinary ones, the kettle and the wind and her mother's feet on the boards, are going out like lamps.

She feels them go. One by one, quietly, in the dark. The voices at the edge of the room. The drip of water from the roof. The rustle of Pebble's feet on her knee. The small steady breath of her brother, at her back. They do not fade. They stop, as a note stops when the string is held, and in the stillness where each one was there is a clean round hollow, like the space where a tooth has been.

I'm sorry, she thinks. I'm sorry. I'm sorry.

She would like to say it aloud. She tries. She opens her mouth and feels the breath go out of her, and there is nothing at all.

* * *

When she wakes she is lying on the cot with a quilt over her, and her mother is crying.

She can see it. Qinghe sits on the edge of the cot with her face in her hands and her shoulders shaking, and her mouth is open, and she is saying something, over and over, in short harsh gasps. Yue cannot hear a word. She lifts a hand and touches her mother's wrist, and Qinghe looks up, and her eyes are red and wild.

Can you hear me? The mouth makes the shape. Yue has to read it, slowly, like a child learning to spell. Yue. Can you hear me?

She shakes her head. Then, because that is cruel, she nods, and smiles, and points to her own ear, and lays her palm flat against her chest. I hear, she tries to say. Not the way you do.

It is a muddle. She sees her mother's face crumple. Behind her, Zhao and Bell and Feng crowd close, all talking at once, a wall of faces with their lips moving, silent as fish. She is overwhelmed. She begins to laugh, because she cannot help it, because it is so absurd, and the laugh comes up out of her chest and goes out into the air, and she cannot hear that either.

Then Pebble speaks.

He is on her pillow. She had not seen him. He is looking at her with his black eyes and his cracked back, and his voice, small and dry, comes straight into her mind, not through her ears but through some other door, as clear as a bell.

I am here, he says. I will always be here. I am a seam. You can hear me.

She stops laughing. She lifts a trembling hand and lays it on his hard round back.

You can hear the seams, he says. Everything that is a door, a gap, a joining. All of it. And me. And if I am very close, and the one I speak to is close to me, I can carry what they say. A pause. I can carry your mother.

She nods. Tears run into the pillow.

Tell her, she thinks. Tell her I'm all right.

She knows, says Pebble. She can see. And then, gently, with a kind of wonder: Yue. Your hair.

She puts up a hand. It is still the same hair, thin and long and gray. But when she looks at her fingers there is a faint silver sheen on them, like frost, and under it a pulse, quick and clear.

Foundation, says Pebble. You have a root. It is the ear. It is the first of its kind. You are going to live a long time, little bell.

* * *

Qinghe does not cry for long.

She is not built for it. By the second day she has wiped her face, set her jaw, and begun a campaign. She sits Yue down in the kitchen with a slate and a stick of chalk, takes a stool opposite, and writes, in large angry strokes, a list: 1. You are alive. 2. You can think. 3. You are, by my count, Foundation Early, which means you have a hundred and forty years if nobody stabs you. 4. I intend to complain at you for all of them.

Yue reads it twice. She laughs. She takes the chalk from her mother's hand and writes underneath, in her own fine small script, I'd expect nothing less.

Qinghe sniffs. She snatches the chalk back and writes: I cannot taste. You cannot hear. We are a fine pair.

We are, Yue writes. It must run in the family.

Her mother looks at the slate for a very long moment. Then she sets it aside, takes Yue's hand, and without a word lays it flat against her own throat.

At first Yue feels nothing but the quick warm pulse of the blood. Then, under it, through the palm, comes a gentle regular tremor, a low flat purr, rising and falling. Qinghe is humming.

It is the tuneless thing she has hummed since Yue was a child. The sound of every morning. It does not reach Yue's ears; it never will. But it reaches her hand, her wrist, her arm, the long bones of her body, and she understands, with a rush of simple wonder, that she can feel the shape of it. She can follow the little falls and lifts. She knows it as well as she ever knew the sound.

Mother, she says, with her hands, with her whole face. Oh, Mother.

Qinghe goes on humming, eyes fixed on the middle distance, and her free hand pats Yue's, once, twice, briskly, as she would pat the head of a stubborn loaf.

* * *

It takes her a month to learn to be deaf, and a year to learn to be whole.

Zhao writes things for her on a slate. Bell invents a language of hands, quick and clever and full of jokes, which half the family learns by the end of the winter. Qinghe, who has never in her life been comfortable with dependence, does it differently: she simply stands in front of Yue when she speaks, with her face turned to the light, and enunciates, ferociously, like a drill sergeant. It works. Yue learns to read lips. She learns to read the way a floor trembles. She learns to read Pebble, who is always there, small and gray and unhurried, and who carries her mother's voice as no one carried a voice before.

She does not mourn it as much as she feared. That is the strangest part. The silence is not an absence. It is a space, and into the space comes a flood of things she had never been able to hear before, because the other noise got in the way. She hears the seams, all of them, in all their keys. She hears the slow turn of the orchard roots. She hears the Mother Tree's daughter, humming to herself in the cold. She can tell which of the Lins is lying, by the tremor in the air around their mouths.

The baby is the hardest.

Kuang is four months old, and the first time Zhao puts him in her arms after the Dock, he laughs. She sees it before she feels it: the wide toothless mouth, the screwed-up eyes, the small body shaking. It is the ordinary, wonderful, helpless laugh of an infant who has just discovered that the world is amusing. She cannot hear it. She stands in the middle of the kitchen with her grandson in her arms and her heart cracking quietly down the middle.

Then he puts his fat hand against her throat, and holds it there, and laughs again.

She feels it this time. A tiny, rapid, fluttering buzz, like a bird under a hand, passing through his palm and up her neck and into the bones of her skull. It is not the sound. It is something else. It is a thing she has never known before, a laugh without an air to carry it, and it is entirely his.

She sits down on the floor with the baby in her lap, in the flour and the wood-chips, and laughs with him until she cries.

And she hears the Gate.

She hears it best at night, in the Dock, sitting on her stool with her back against the wall, while her brother feeds the Seed and Tian Mo stands watch in the shadows. It is a deep slow sound, a long breath, the sound of something very large and very patient, turning over in its sleep. She has heard it all her life without knowing. Now she hears it clearly.

And she hears that it is not alone.

It happens on the sixtieth night. She is dozing, her head tilted back, her hand resting on Pebble's cracked spine, and the Gate's breath comes in and out, in and out. She half dreams of her father. Then, between two breaths, something else comes through: very thin, very faint, as from a very long way off, a voice she has never heard before.

It is a man's voice. It is tired, and kind, and a little frightened.

Is it all right? it says. Is the child all right?

She sits bolt upright.

Brother, she thinks, Jian, but he is bent over the Seed with his eyes closed and his lips moving, counting, and he does not turn. She reaches for Pebble. He is looking at the wall.

I heard it, he says. I did not know whether to say.

Who is it?

The voice comes again, so soft it is hardly a sound at all. It is the voice of someone talking in his sleep, from the bottom of a deep and dreaming night.

Is the child all right? Please. Somebody. Is he all right?
